pos.note: ὁ points out one man. Greek counts the article as a part of speech, and Latin has none.
τῇ points out the land, and the dative goes with ἐν. The article is a part of speech in Greek.
φύλαξ names the watchman, and it is the subject of πέμπει.
δῶρον names the gift, and it is the object of πέμπει.
λῡ́ει says what the man does. It is the present, third person singular, of λῡ́ω (§383).
ἐστι says what the victory is. The form has no accent of its own, because it leans on ἀγαθή (§183).

pos.orig: The good man looses the horse.
pos.note: ἀγαθός tells what sort of man, and it adheres to ἄνθρωπος.
ἀγαθή tells what sort of victory, across the verb. Before the enclitic it keeps the acute (§183).
σοφῶς tells how he writes. An adverb in -ως keeps one form (§343, §345).

pos.orig: The king rules the men badly.
pos.note: κακῶς tells how he rules. Smyth prints κακῶς, and the gloss there is ill (§343).
ἐν stands before the noun and puts χώρᾳ in the dative (§1687).

pos.orig: He sends the horse into the land.
pos.note: εἰς stands before the noun and puts χώρᾱν in the accusative (§1686).

pos.s: ὁ φύλαξ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως πέμπει τὸ δῶρον
pos.orig: The watchman sends the gift out of the city.
pos.note: ἐκ stands before the noun and puts πόλεως in the genitive (§1688).

pos.s: ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ ὁ κριτὴς λῡ́ουσι τὸν ἵππον
pos.orig: The man and the judge loose the horse.
pos.note: καί joins the man and the judge. In this sentence it is a conjunction (§2868).

pos.s: ὁ ἄνθρωπος λῡ́ει τὸν ἵππον, ἀλλὰ ὁ κριτὴς γράφει
pos.orig: The man looses the horse, but the judge writes.
pos.note: ἀλλά joins the two statements, and the second is set against the first (§2775).

pos.orig: For the man looses the horse.
pos.note: γάρ means for, and it is a causal conjunction. It stands after the first word (§2803, §2810).
ἐγώ stands in for the speaker, and it is the subject. The nominative is ἐγώ (§325).
ἐμοί stands in for the person who is trusted. It is the dative of ἐγώ (§325).

pos.s: ὁ λῡ́ων τὸν ἵππον ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός ἐστι
pos.orig: The man who is loosing the horse is good.
pos.note: λῡ́ων depends on ἄνθρωπος and keeps the time of the verb. It is the present participle of λῡ́ω (§305).

pos.orig: The judge writes, educating the young man.
pos.note: παιδεύων depends on κριτής and keeps the time of the verb. Smyth prints παιδεύων, educating (§305).

pos.orig: Alas, the man looses the horse.
pos.note: φεῦ is a cry of grief. It neither names a thing nor joins a statement (§1407, §904).
φεῦ is a cry, and the genitive gives the cause. Smyth prints φεῦ τοῦ ἀνδρός (§1407).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
ds: Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: ἄνθρωπος is a noun. It takes endings for case and number (§231).

decline.s: ὁ φύλαξ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως πέμπει τὸ δῶρον
decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
ds: Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: πόλεως is a noun, the genitive of πόλις. It takes endings for case and number (§268).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: λῡ́ει is a verb. It takes endings for person, number, and tense (§383).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: ἐστι is a verb. It takes endings for person, number, and tense (§768).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: ἀγαθός is an adjective. It takes the endings of the noun, and an adjective takes degrees (§287).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: ἀληθής is an adjective. It takes endings for case and number, and an adjective takes degrees (§292).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: ἐγώ is a pronoun. It still shows case: ἐγώ, ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ (§325).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: ἐμοί is a pronoun, the dative of ἐγώ. The case is still marked (§325).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
decline.why: σοφῶς is an adverb. It keeps one form (§343).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
decline.why: κακῶς is an adverb. It keeps one form. Smyth prints it from κακῶν (§343).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: ἐν is a preposition. It keeps one form, and it governs the dative (§1687).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: εἰς is a preposition. It keeps one form, and it governs the accusative (§1686).

decline.s: ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ ὁ κριτὴς λῡ́ουσι τὸν ἵππον
decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: καί is a conjunction. It keeps one form (§2868).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: γάρ is a conjunction. It keeps one form (§2810).

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
ds: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: φεῦ is an interjection, a cry, and it keeps one form (§1407).

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: ἄνθρωπος is the subject of λῡ́ει. The subject stands in the nominative.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: φύλαξ is the subject of πέμπει. The subject stands in the nominative (§256).

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: ἵππον is the object of λῡ́ει. The object stands in the accusative.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: βασιλέᾱ is the object of παιδεύει. The accusative singular of βασιλεύς is βασιλέᾱ (§275).

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: βασιλέως marks the owner of the horse. That is the genitive of possession (§1297).

cases.s: ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀπὸ τῆς θαλάττης πέμπει τὸ δῶρον
cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: ἀπό takes the genitive, and the phrase marks separation (§1684). Greek has no ablative.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: ἄρχω takes the genitive of the people ruled (§1370). Smyth's example is the infinitive ἄρχειν, and ἄρχει has the thematic ending of §383.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: κριτῇ is the person to whom the gift is sent. That person stands in the dative (§1469).

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: λίθῳ is the means. The dative of means needs no preposition (§1507).

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: ἡμέρᾳ is the time when. The dative of time when usually has an attributive, here μακρᾷ (§1539).

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: ἄνθρωπε is the person addressed. Smyth prints the vocative without ὦ (§1283).

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: βασιλεῦ is the person addressed. The nominative is βασιλεύς (§275).

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: κριτά is the vocative of κριτής, and it is the person addressed (§222). Before the next word the acute is written as a grave (§154).

govern.why: ἐν takes the dative only (§1687). χώρᾳ is the dative of χώρᾱ.
εἰς takes the accusative only (§1686). χώρᾱν is the accusative of χώρᾱ.

govern.s: ὁ φύλαξ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως πέμπει τὸ δῶρον
govern.why: ἐκ takes the genitive only (§1688). Before a consonant the form is ἐκ (§136).
ἐξ is the form of ἐκ before a vowel (§136), and it takes the genitive (§1688). ὁδοῦ is the genitive of ὁδός.

govern.s: ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀπὸ τῆς θαλάττης πέμπει τὸ δῶρον
govern.why: ἀπό takes the genitive only (§1684). The phrase marks separation.
σύν takes the dative only (§1696). In Attic prose outside Xenophon, μετά with the genitive is the usual word, and σύν survives in old formulas and in Xenophon.

govern.q: What case does πρός take here?
govern.why: In this sentence πρός marks motion toward, and that use takes the accusative (§1695.3). πρός takes other cases in other senses.

govern.q: What case does ὑπό take for the personal agent?
govern.why: With a passive verb, ὑπό takes the genitive of the personal agent (§1698). λῡ́εται is the present passive, and the form is the same as the present middle (§383).

govern.q: What case does ἄρχω take for the people ruled?
govern.why: A verb of ruling takes the genitive (§1370). Smyth's example is the infinitive ἄρχειν. The finite form ἄρχει has the thematic ending of §383.
πιστεύω takes the dative (§1745). ἐμοί is the dative of ἐγώ (§325).

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: ἄνθρωπος is masculine, nominative, singular. ἀγαθός matches it in gender, number, and case.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: ὁδός is feminine, though it ends in -ος. ἀγαθή is the feminine nominative, and it matches.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: δῶρον is neuter, nominative, singular. ἀγαθόν matches it.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: ὁδός is feminine. ἀληθής is the feminine form as well as the masculine, because the adjective has two endings (§292).

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: ὁδός is feminine. ἀγαθός is masculine, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Case and number match.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: θάλαττα is feminine. μακρός is masculine, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Case and number match.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: ἐλπίς is feminine. σοφόν is neuter, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Case and number match.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: βασιλεύς is masculine. κακή is feminine, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Case and number match.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: ἄνθρωπος is singular and ἀγαθοί is plural. Gender and case match.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: νῖκαι is plural and ἀγαθή is singular. Gender and case match.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: πόλις is singular and ἀληθεῖς is plural. The adjective has two endings, so the feminine plural is ἀληθεῖς, and the fault is number.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: δῶρα is plural and κακόν is singular. Gender and case match.

agree.a: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
agree.why: ἵππος is nominative and ἀγαθοῦ is genitive. Gender and number match.

agree.a: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
agree.why: νῑ́κη is nominative and ἀγαθῇ is dative. Gender and number match.

agree.a: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
agree.why: ὁδός is nominative, and it is feminine. μακράν is accusative. Gender and number match.

agree.a: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
agree.why: κριτής is nominative and σοφῷ is dative. Gender and number match.

produce.why: χωρῶν is the genitive plural of χώρᾱ (§216).
νῑ́κης is the genitive singular of νῑ́κη (§216).
θαλάττης is the genitive singular of θάλαττα (§216).
μοίρᾱς is the accusative plural of μοῖρα (§216).
νεᾱνίου is the genitive singular of νεᾱνίᾱς (§222).
κριτά is the vocative singular of κριτής (§222).
ἵπποις is the dative plural of ἵππος (§231).
ἄνθρωπε is the vocative singular of ἄνθρωπος (§231).
ὁδοῦ is the genitive singular of ὁδός (§231).
δῶρα is the nominative plural of δῶρον (§231).
φύλακι is the dative singular of φύλαξ (§256).
ἐλπίδα is the accusative singular of ἐλπίς (§257).
σώματος is the genitive singular of σῶμα (§258).
πόλεως is the genitive singular of πόλις (§268).
βασιλέᾱ is the accusative singular of βασιλεύς (§275).

produce.lemmaLine: λῡ́ω, λῡ́σω, ἔλῡσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην, loose
produce.want: present active indicative, third person singular
produce.why: λῡ́ει is the present active indicative, third person singular, of λῡ́ω (§383).

produce.lemmaLine: λῡ́ω, λῡ́σω, ἔλῡσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην, loose
produce.want: imperfect active indicative, third person singular
produce.why: ἔλῡε is the imperfect active indicative, third person singular, of λῡ́ω (§383).

produce.lemmaLine: λῡ́ω, λῡ́σω, ἔλῡσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην, loose
produce.want: future active indicative, third person singular
produce.why: λῡ́σει is the future active indicative, third person singular, of λῡ́ω (§383).

produce.lemmaLine: λῡ́ω, λῡ́σω, ἔλῡσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην, loose
produce.want: aorist active indicative, third person singular
produce.why: ἔλῡσε is the aorist active indicative, third person singular, of λῡ́ω (§383).

produce.lemmaLine: λῡ́ω, λῡ́σω, ἔλῡσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην, loose
produce.want: aorist active indicative, first person plural
produce.why: ἐλῡ́σαμεν is the aorist active indicative, first person plural, of λῡ́ω (§383).

produce.lemmaLine: λῡ́ω, λῡ́σω, ἔλῡσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην, loose
produce.want: present active indicative, third person plural
produce.why: λῡ́ουσι is the present active indicative, third person plural, of λῡ́ω (§383).

produce.lemmaLine: λῡ́ω, λῡ́σω, ἔλῡσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην, loose
produce.want: present middle indicative, third person singular
produce.why: λῡ́εται is the present middle indicative, third person singular (§383). The same form is the present passive.

produce.want: present active indicative, third person singular
produce.why: ἐστί is the present, third person singular, of εἰμί (§768). This is the dictionary form. In a sentence the accent follows the enclitic rules (§183).

produce.want: imperfect active indicative, third person singular
produce.why: ἦν is the imperfect, third person singular, of εἰμί (§768). The first person singular may be ἦ or ἦν. This answer is the third person, which is only ἦν.

cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The article, the noun, and the object fit, and the finite verb finishes the sentence.

cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The adjective fits the noun, and ἐστι finishes the sentence.

cong.s: ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ γράφει
cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: ἐν fits the dative, and the finite verb finishes the sentence.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The adjective fits the noun. There is no verb, so the sense is not finished.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: ἐν fits the dative. There is no verb, so the sense is not finished.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: ἄνθρωπε is the vocative (§1283). A vocative by itself does not finish a sentence (§904).

cong.a: Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
cong.why: κριταί is plural and λῡ́ει is singular. The parts do not fit.

cong.a: Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
cong.why: θάλαττα is feminine, and ὁ is masculine. The adjective fits the noun, and the article does not, so the construction fails.

cong.a: Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
cong.why: τόν is accusative and ἵππος is nominative. The two do not agree, so the construction fails.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form Attic does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: λῡ́ωμι is not an Attic form. The present, first person singular, of λῡ́ω is λῡ́ω (§383). The fault is in the one word.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form Attic does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: δώρονες is not an Attic form. The nominative plural of δῶρον is δῶρα (§231). The article and the adjective are real forms, and the fault is in the one word.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form Attic does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: ἔλῡσανε is not an Attic form. The aorist, third person plural, is ἔλῡσαν (§383). Movable ν is not added to that ending (§134).

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: οἱ is a real plural article, and ἄνθρωπος is a real singular noun. The two do not agree in number, so the join fails.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: ἀγαθός is a real adjective, and it is masculine. νῑ́κη is feminine, so the two do not agree. The fault is in the join.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: τῷ is a real dative, and ἵππον is a real accusative. The two do not agree in case, so the join fails.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: λῡ́ουσι is a real plural form (§383). The subject ἄνθρωπος is singular, so the verb does not fit it.
